newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile seen needing more rain to end power shortage.
newsitem.headline: Chile seen needing more rain to end power shortage.

text.p: Heavy rainfall in Chile this weekend has eased the country's drought conditions but it will take more precipitation in the coming weeks before power rationing can be ruled out, electric industry analysts said.

"The rains are definitely positive news, but we are not in the clear by any means," said Colin Curvey, an analyst at brokerage Celfin. "The dams are recovering somewhat but they still have very little water compared with a normal year."

The drought has threatened to cut into power utility profits and drive down share prices by forcing hydroelectric generators to buy electricity on the spot market as their reservoirs dry up. Big hydroelectric operators affected by the drought include Endesa, its parent company Enersis SA and Colbun SA.
The national meteorological service forecast light showers to continue for the next couple of days in central and southern Chile -- the regions most affected by the drought.
News of the heavy rains sparked a rally in electricity stocks in Santiago and New York, with Endesa climbing nearly two percent to 263 pesos Monday and rising to 264.5 pesos at midsession Tuesday.
But the drought is not over. The government announced Monday it would extend emergency measures, including a five percent voltage reduction, for another month.
Officials have warned they would impose rationing if water levels in reservoirs do not rise. Hydroelectric power from reservoirs normally accounts for about 65 percent of central Chile's supply.
While water levels have almost returned to normal at some dams, the levels are still extremely low at others, said Eleonor Lefebure, an analyst at Santander Investments.
"We are still looking at dry conditions and the system is still tight," said Lefebure.
"If it rains normally, then we should be OK -- just. The drought now seems remote but this doesn't mean we won't have rationing."

Endesa's Laja reservoir -- the largest dam in the central rid -- has enough water to operate at just four percent generating capacity, Lefebure said. The dam usually operates at half of its full capacity.

The drought is said to be Chile's worst this century. Figures from the national meteorological service show Santiago becoming a steadily drier city since the turn of the century, with average annual rainfall dropping from about 410 mm in 1905 to about 310 mm today.
Companies have been forced to buy more expensive power from coal-fired producers to meet their supply contracts.
